analysis.one_liner: Raises fines and prison terms for companies caught illegally employing children and forces annual public reporting on violators.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise child labor penalties and require annual public reporting of violators was referred to committee and never received a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to make it much costlier to employ children illegally. Civil fines would rise from a maximum of $11,000 per violation to as much as $150,000, and up to $700,000 when a violation kills a child worker, with penalties doubled for repeat or willful violators [S2]. Repeat violators could face up to 5 years in prison, and up to 10 years when a child is seriously hurt or killed [S2]. The Labor Department would also have to publish a yearly report naming every employer found to have violated child labor law, listing the consumer brands made with illegal child labor, and describing violation trends and enforcement gaps [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Child workers, especially the growing number of minors found working overnight shifts, in meatpacking plants, and in hazardous jobs in violation of federal law, gain stronger legal protection. Honest employers also benefit from public reporting that levels the field against competitors who cut costs by employing children illegally.

how_it_helps.text: Raises maximum civil penalties for child labor violations from $11,000 to $150,000 per violation, and to $700,000 where a child dies, with penalties doubled for repeated or willful violations.

Creates new criminal penalties of up to 5 years in prison and $100,000 fines for repeat or willful child labor violations, and up to 10 years and $500,000 when a violation kills or seriously injures a worker under 18.

Requires the Labor Department to publish an annual report naming violators, the consumer brands made with illegal child labor, violation trends by industry and region, and what enforcement resources are needed—giving families and consumers visibility into which companies employ children.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that employ children illegally would pay sharply higher fines, face possible prison terms for repeat or deadly violations, and have their names and consumer brands listed publicly each year. Consumers might indirectly pay slightly more where violators raised prices to cover compliance costs.

drawbacks.text: Higher fines and prison terms raise compliance costs for industries that legally employ 16- and 17-year-olds, and some employers argue penalties could be triggered by paperwork mistakes rather than true exploitation, especially for small businesses.
Publicly naming violators and listing associated consumer brands before due process is complete could expose companies to reputational harm from contested or preliminary findings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits—stiffer penalties and public accountability for companies that employ children illegally—would fall on a narrow set of violators, and the costs to compliant businesses are negligible. The main honest objection is that penalties alone do not fix detection: child labor violations are found only when investigators look, and the bill's reporting requirement itself acknowledges that enforcement resources may need to grow. Even so, the bill's costs are small and its protections direct.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: H.R. 2956 was introduced on April 27, 2023 and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
No further action was taken: no hearings, no markup, no floor vote appear in the bill's action history for the remainder of the Congress.
The bill attracted 42 Democratic cosponsors in the House but no Republican cosponsors, and the House was controlled by Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that illegally employ children, and any firms that benefit from weak enforcement, are better off; child workers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who use illegal child labor

for.name: Rep. Daniel Kildee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise child labor penalties and require annual reporting.

for.name: 42 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor signed on.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral—no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the action history—leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 42 cosponsors were Democrats, no Republicans sponsored or cosponsored it, and the Republican-controlled committee declined to move it.

industries.industry: Staffing and cleaning services, food processing, meatpacking, and construction firms that rely on underage workers
industries.note: These industries have faced rising federal child labor findings; the bill would make violations far more expensive, with fines up to $700,000 per death and possible prison time, and would name violators and their consumer brands publicly each year.
Compliant businesses face little direct cost, though higher penalty exposure and public reporting raise the stakes of any misclassification or record-keeping error involving young workers.
